paper_metadata.title: Quantum Monte Carlo Integration: The Full Advantage in Minimal Circuit Depth

summary: This paper proposes Fourier QMCI, a gate-based amplitude-estimation method that preserves the full quadratic MSE scaling Θ(q^-2) of QAE while avoiding quantum arithmetic by decomposing the target function into Fourier components. In the numerical proof-of-principle on a 16-point distribution, Fourier QMCI achieved an RMSE fit of 194 q^-1.02, compared with 107 q^-1.05 for conventional QMCI and a reported rescaled-QMCI scaling of about q^-0.771; the crossover with classical MCI occurred at about 1100 uses of P and 8 sequential uses of Q.

experiments.description: Theoretical and simulated proof-of-principle experiment for Fourier-based quantum Monte Carlo integration on a 16-point univariate probability distribution, comparing Fourier QMCI against classical MCI, rescaled QMCI, and conventional QMCI with quantum arithmetic.

algorithm.variant: Fourier QMCI using QAE subroutines on Fourier-series components; QPE-free amplitude estimation

hyperparameters.qae_variant: not specified; any QAE algorithm satisfying MSE ~ q^-lambda
hyperparameters.lambda: convergence rate of underlying QAE algorithm
hyperparameters.qn: q0 * n^-kappa for univariate Fourier terms
hyperparameters.periodic_extension: piecewise periodic function with matching value and first derivative at boundaries

problem_formulation.encoding_details: A circuit P prepares a quantum state |p> encoding a discrete multivariate probability distribution; the ith marginal is probed by applying controlled Ry rotations proportional to n*omega*x(i)+beta on an ancilla qubit.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Estimate mu = E(f(X)) for X ~ p(x(i)); in the numerical example, f(x)=x and the target is the mean of a 16-point distribution.

problem_instance.description: Univariate 16-point probability distribution supported on {-8,-7,...,7}; used to compare Fourier QMCI, rescaled QMCI, conventional QMCI with quantum arithmetic, and classical MCI.

dataset_specification.description: 16-point distribution shown in Fig. 2(a); mean not equal to median to avoid artificially favorable rescaled-QMCI behavior

problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Simulated results averaged over 500 runs; RMSE plotted versus number of uses of P; line-of-best-fit slopes reported for Fourier QMCI, rescaled QMCI, and quantum-arithmetic QMCI.

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Fourier coefficients of the periodic extension are assumed symbolically computable or precomputed; the paper notes that numerical integration of coefficients would shift, not reduce, complexity.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Classical recombination of estimated Fourier coefficients; RMSE fitting and comparison to classical baselines.

convergence_data.loss_curve_shape: RMSE decreases approximately as a power law; reported slope for Fourier QMCI is about -1.02 on log-log plot

results.unit: sequential uses of Q in a single circuit
data points in the synthetic distribution

speedup_claims.conditions: for Fourier QMCI with QAE subroutines satisfying MSE ~ q^-lambda; full quadratic advantage retained without quantum arithmetic
speedup_claims.caveats: Requires symbolic or precomputed Fourier coefficients; assumes suitable smooth periodic extension and shallow-depth state preparation.

speedup_claims.factor: better than classical MCI and rescaled QMCI at sufficiently small desired RMSE
speedup_claims.baseline_method: classical monte carlo integration and rescaled qmci
speedup_claims.caveats: Cross-over occurs only after enough uses of P; constant factor is larger than conventional QMCI.

speedup_claims.factor: same asymptotic rate as conventional QMCI with quantum arithmetic
speedup_claims.conditions: asymptotically, both scale with MSE Theta(q^-lambda)
speedup_claims.caveats: Fourier QMCI has a larger constant factor in the numerical example (194 vs 107 in RMSE fit).

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: Theta(q^-lambda) MSE with q uses of the state-preparation circuit P; total query count q_tot in Theta(q0) for the constructed Fourier decomposition scheme
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: Classical Monte Carlo MSE Theta(q^-1) for the comparable mean-estimation setting
complexity_analysis.constant_factor_quantum: For the numerical example, Fourier QMCI RMSE fit constant 194 (RMSE = 194 q^-1.02)
complexity_analysis.total_operations_quantum: q_tot in Theta(q0); in the numerical example crossover occurs at about 1100 uses of P and circuit depth 8 sequential uses of Q in a single circuit
complexity_analysis.crossover_n: Approximately 1100 uses of P for the numerical example

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: About 1100 uses of P for the simulated crossover; 8 sequential uses of Q in a single circuit.
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: A shallow state-preparation circuit P for a 16-point distribution, plus QAE subroutines on Fourier components; the paper assumes symbolic or precomputed Fourier coefficients and does not report hardware resources.
limiting_factors: Requires symbolic or precomputed Fourier coefficients
Crossover shown only on a 16-point toy distribution
State preparation and QAE depth remain nontrivial

notes: Hardware type inferred as simulator_other because the paper reports simulated numerical results and no real QPU/device is named.
Circuit depth 8 is reported in the discussion of the crossover point as '8 sequential uses of Q in any single quantum circuit.'
The paper is primarily theoretical; the numerical section is a simulation proof-of-principle rather than a hardware run.
The paper presents a theoretical method and simulated proof-of-principle results, not a hardware demonstration.
It reports asymptotic quadratic advantage in MSE, but no practical advantage over classical methods on a meaningful real-world benchmark.
